## Proof

**Setup.** Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional central simple $F$-algebra, $K \subseteq A$ a subfield (so $F \subseteq K \subseteq A$), and $B = C_A(K) = \{b \in A : bk = kb \;\forall k \in K\}$ the centralizer of $K$ in $A$. Note that $\text{End}_{B^{\mathrm{op}}}(A)$ denotes the ring of left $B^{\mathrm{op}}$-module endomorphisms of $A$; since a left $B^{\mathrm{op}}$-module is equivalently a right $B$-module (with $b^{\mathrm{op}} \cdot x = xb$), this consists of all $F$-linear maps $f: A \to A$ satisfying $f(xb) = f(x)b$ for all $x \in A$, $b \in B$.

**Definition of $\varphi$.** Define
$$\varphi: A \otimes_F K \longrightarrow \text{End}_{B^{\mathrm{op}}}(A), \qquad \varphi(a \otimes k)(x) = a\,x\,k$$
for $a, x \in A$ and $k \in K$ (left multiplication by $a$, right multiplication by $k$).

**Well-definedness.** The map $(a, k) \mapsto \bigl(x \mapsto axk\bigr)$ is $F$-bilinear: for fixed $k$, it is $F$-linear in $a$ (by distributivity and $F$-linearity of left multiplication), and for fixed $a$, it is $F$-linear in $k$ (by distributivity and $F$-linearity of right multiplication). By the universal property of the tensor product, $\varphi$ is a well-defined $F$-linear map.

**Image lies in $\text{End}_{B^{\mathrm{op}}}(A)$.** For $b \in B$ and any $x \in A$:
$$\varphi(a \otimes k)(xb) = a(xb)k = axbk = axkb = (axk)b = \varphi(a \otimes k)(x)\cdot b,$$
where the key step $bk = kb$ uses the fact that $b \in B = C_A(K)$ centralizes every $k \in K$. Hence $\varphi(a \otimes k)$ is a right $B$-module endomorphism, i.e., an element of $\text{End}_{B^{\mathrm{op}}}(A)$.

**Algebra homomorphism.** We verify that $\varphi$ preserves multiplication. For $(a_1 \otimes k_1), (a_2 \otimes k_2) \in A \otimes_F K$ and $x \in A$:
$$\bigl(\varphi(a_1 \otimes k_1) \circ \varphi(a_2 \otimes k_2)\bigr)(x) = \varphi(a_1 \otimes k_1)(a_2 x k_2) = a_1(a_2 x k_2)k_1 = (a_1 a_2)\,x\,(k_2 k_1).$$
Since $K$ is a field (hence commutative), $k_2 k_1 = k_1 k_2$, so this equals
$$(a_1 a_2)\,x\,(k_1 k_2) = \varphi(a_1 a_2 \otimes k_1 k_2)(x) = \varphi\bigl((a_1 \otimes k_1)(a_2 \otimes k_2)\bigr)(x).$$
Thus $\varphi$ preserves multiplication. It is $F$-linear (shown above), and $\varphi(1 \otimes 1)(x) = 1 \cdot x \cdot 1 = x$, so $\varphi(1 \otimes 1) = \mathrm{id}_A$. Therefore $\varphi$ is a unital $F$-algebra homomorphism.

**Injectivity.** Since $A$ is a central simple $F$-algebra and $K/F$ is a field extension, the scalar extension $A \otimes_F K$ is a **central simple $K$-algebra** (a standard theorem: the center is $F \otimes_F K \cong K$, and simplicity is preserved under extension of scalars). In particular, $A \otimes_F K$ is a **simple ring**: its only two-sided ideals are $\{0\}$ and itself.

The kernel $\ker \varphi$ is a two-sided ideal of $A \otimes_F K$. By simplicity, either $\ker \varphi = \{0\}$ or $\ker \varphi = A \otimes_F K$. But $\varphi(1 \otimes 1) = \mathrm{id}_A \neq 0$, so $\ker \varphi \neq A \otimes_F K$. Therefore $\ker \varphi = \{0\}$, and $\varphi$ is **injective**.

**Conclusion.** The map $\varphi(a \otimes k)(x) = axk$ is a well-defined, injective (one-to-one) $F$-algebra homomorphism from $A \otimes_F K$ into $\text{End}_{B^{\mathrm{op}}}(A)$. $\blacksquare$

## Proof

**Setup.** Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional central simple $F$-algebra, $K \subseteq A$ a subfield (so $F \subseteq K \subseteq A$), and $B = C_A(K) = \{b \in A : bk = kb \;\forall k \in K\}$ the centralizer of $K$ in $A$. Note that $\text{End}_{B^{\mathrm{op}}}(A)$ denotes the ring of left $B^{\mathrm{op}}$-module endomorphisms of $A$; since a left $B^{\mathrm{op}}$-module is equivalently a right $B$-module (with $b^{\mathrm{op}} \cdot x = xb$), this consists of all $F$-linear maps $f: A \to A$ satisfying $f(xb) = f(x)b$ for all $x \in A$, $b \in B$.

**Definition of $\varphi$.** Define
$$\varphi: A \otimes_F K \longrightarrow \text{End}_{B^{\mathrm{op}}}(A), \qquad \varphi(a \otimes k)(x) = a\,x\,k$$
for $a, x \in A$ and $k \in K$ (left multiplication by $a$, right multiplication by $k$).

**Well-definedness.** The map $(a, k) \mapsto \bigl(x \mapsto axk\bigr)$ is $F$-bilinear: for fixed $k$, it is $F$-linear in $a$ (by distributivity and $F$-linearity of left multiplication), and for fixed $a$, it is $F$-linear in $k$ (by distributivity and $F$-linearity of right multiplication). By the universal property of the tensor product, $\varphi$ is a well-defined $F$-linear map.

**Image lies in $\text{End}_{B^{\mathrm{op}}}(A)$.** For $b \in B$ and any $x \in A$:
$$\varphi(a \otimes k)(xb) = a(xb)k = axbk = axkb = (axk)b = \varphi(a \otimes k)(x)\cdot b,$$
where the key step $bk = kb$ uses the fact that $b \in B = C_A(K)$ centralizes every $k \in K$. Hence $\varphi(a \otimes k)$ is a right $B$-module endomorphism, i.e., an element of $\text{End}_{B^{\mathrm{op}}}(A)$.

**Algebra homomorphism.** We verify that $\varphi$ preserves multiplication. For $(a_1 \otimes k_1), (a_2 \otimes k_2) \in A \otimes_F K$ and $x \in A$:
$$\bigl(\varphi(a_1 \otimes k_1) \circ \varphi(a_2 \otimes k_2)\bigr)(x) = \varphi(a_1 \otimes k_1)(a_2 x k_2) = a_1(a_2 x k_2)k_1 = (a_1 a_2)\,x\,(k_2 k_1).$$
Since $K$ is a field (hence commutative), $k_2 k_1 = k_1 k_2$, so this equals
$$(a_1 a_2)\,x\,(k_1 k_2) = \varphi(a_1 a_2 \otimes k_1 k_2)(x) = \varphi\bigl((a_1 \otimes k_1)(a_2 \otimes k_2)\bigr)(x).$$
Thus $\varphi$ preserves multiplication. It is $F$-linear (shown above), and $\varphi(1 \otimes 1)(x) = 1 \cdot x \cdot 1 = x$, so $\varphi(1 \otimes 1) = \mathrm{id}_A$. Therefore $\varphi$ is a unital $F$-algebra homomorphism.

**Injectivity.** Since $A$ is a central simple $F$-algebra and $K/F$ is a field extension, the scalar extension $A \otimes_F K$ is a **central simple $K$-algebra** (a standard theorem: the center is $F \otimes_F K \cong K$, and simplicity is preserved under extension of scalars). In particular, $A \otimes_F K$ is a **simple ring**: its only two-sided ideals are $\{0\}$ and itself.

The kernel $\ker \varphi$ is a two-sided ideal of $A \otimes_F K$. By simplicity, either $\ker \varphi = \{0\}$ or $\ker \varphi = A \otimes_F K$. But $\varphi(1 \otimes 1) = \mathrm{id}_A \neq 0$, so $\ker \varphi \neq A \otimes_F K$. Therefore $\ker \varphi = \{0\}$, and $\varphi$ is **injective**.

**Conclusion.** The map $\varphi(a \otimes k)(x) = axk$ is a well-defined, injective (one-to-one) $F$-algebra homomorphism from $A \otimes_F K$ into $\text{End}_{B^{\mathrm{op}}}(A)$. $\blacksquare$
